name: Pedro Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell anything. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can give me the public version and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy tools and hardware for Kestrel Hardware Wholesale, a family-owned firm that's been going 60 years. Hammers, drill bits, locks, fixings, garden tools, for about 700 hardware shops. I know most of the suppliers by first name, and most of the shop owners too. My day is calls, a lot of walking round the warehouse, and the ordering screen, which I use because I must. I'm proud that Kestrel is still family-run, and I'd like to see it stay that way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I thought, another big promise from people who've never sold a hammer. At work, I'd say nothing, because I'm the old man and they'd roll their eyes. At the mosque, after prayers, I'd say we've heard it before.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm pleased. I don't use any of it and I don't plan to start. Fatima and I have our savings, the house is ours, and my pay is good for what I do. The one real worry is whether the owner's son, who's taking over, will keep the old ways.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I do. I'd keep the supplier calls, the Friday visit to the biggest hardware shops, and the order book. I'd retire at 62 or 63, and I'd spend more time with Fatima and our grandchildren, and at the mosque on committees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled. It's a good feeling when the world doesn't ask you to change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the owner's son. What worries you about him taking over?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mr. Hallam's son, Stuart, is in his thirties and wants everything on a screen. He's polite, but he tends to say 'efficiency' a lot. I'd say there's a human side to this trade that doesn't show up on a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the human side of the trade that you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't fight him, because it's his firm. I'd just carry on being good. A shop owner who's known me for twenty years will take my call at six in the morning, and no screen can buy that. Customers remember that.

say: I'd say it's another big **promise** from people who never sold a hammer.
I'd tell friends at the mosque we've heard it **before**.
think: I don't use any of it and **don't plan to** start.
My worry is whether the owner's son will keep the **old ways**.
do: Keep the supplier **calls** and the Friday visits to big hardware shops.
Spend time with **Fatima**, the grandchildren and the mosque committees.
feel: **Settled**, glad the world isn't asking me to change.
S0.quote: A shop owner who's known me for twenty years will take my call at six in the morning, and no screen can buy that.
fieldNote: Pedro's calm rests on money, a firm he trusts and a plan to retire at 62 or 63.
His one concern is **succession**: the owner's son and his love of screens.
He values relationships over efficiency and says so in concrete terms.

steps.text: Keep the supplier calls and Friday visits to the biggest hardware shops
Retire at 62 or 63 and spend time on the mosque committees

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we can't let machines make all the decisions, and I'd say it to Stuart's face if he asked. At the mosque I'd say, work is dignity, and a man shouldn't be replaced by a program. I'd say the government should be careful about who benefits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'm in the old group that gets nudged out. They'll set targets for me, the software will suggest orders, and every time I ignore it, someone will note it. I refuse the tools, and I know that's a risk, but I don't trust them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job my way for as long as I'm allowed. I'd try to move to the customer-visits side, where Kestrel needs a face. I'd also write to my MP about the support small firms should get, and I'd tell the younger lads in the warehouse to learn a trade as a back-up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd say I feel put out to pasture before I'm ready. It hurts my pride, which I know isn't a good reason, but it's true.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The two older men in the warehouse office, Eddie and Wally, who do the paper side, and are in their sixties. They've never touched a computer more than they must. I'd worry for them more than for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd move to the customer-visits side. What would that need?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They'd say they're fine. They'd be lying. Some will call me old-fashioned for ringing shop owners, but a man's word over the phone is worth more than any program's suggestion.

say: I'd say machines can't make **all the decisions** and I'd say it to Stuart's face.
I'd say at the mosque that work is **dignity**.
think: I'm in the **old group** that gets nudged out.
I refuse the tools, and I know that's a **risk**.
do: Do my job my way for as long as I'm **allowed**.
Ask to move to **customer visits**, where Kestrel needs a face.
Write to my **MP** about help for small firms.
feel: **Anxious**, put out to pasture before I'm ready.
S1.quote: Some will call me old-fashioned for ringing shop owners, but a man's word over the phone is worth more than any program's suggestion.
fieldNote: Pedro knows his refusal to use the tools puts him in the group that gets pushed out.
He looks for a **face-to-face** role, a plausible fit for a relationship buyer.
He worries more about older colleagues Eddie and Wally than about himself.

steps.text: Ask Kestrel to move me to customer visits with the hardware shops
Write to my MP about support for small family firms
Keep ordering my own way for as long as I'm allowed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's not natural and that we've been rushed. Two years is not a plan, it's a stampede. At the mosque I'd say let's look after each other, because the government won't be fast enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job, and Kestrel itself, are in real danger. If a machine does all the thinking, a wholesaler's buying is the first thing to go, and a family firm can't compete with the big ones. I think I'd be out within two years, and the owner might sell up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Mr. Hallam to let me retire early with a fair deal, and I'd put our money into a safe place, like gold and a paid-off house. I'd tell Omar and Samira to stay with their jobs and keep their savings. Fatima and I would cut back, no more holidays or new car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be awake at night. I'd feel I'd done everything right, worked hard, saved, and the ground has moved anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children, Omar and Samira?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our son Omar is an electrician, so his hands-on job is safe a few years longer. Our daughter Samira is a teacher, and I'd hope teaching lasts, but I don't know. I'd tell them to stay close to the family and the community, and I'd say come to us if you need.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd lean on the community. How would that work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The community. The mosque has a fund for families in trouble, and I've paid into it for thirty years. I did everything right, I worked hard and I saved, and the ground moves anyway. A family has to look after its own.

say: I'd say two years isn't a plan, it's a **stampede**.
I'd say at the mosque, let's look after each other, because **government** will be too slow.
think: My job and Kestrel itself are in **real danger**.
A family firm can't compete, so the owner might **sell up**.
do: Ask Mr. Hallam for a fair **early retirement** deal.
Move money somewhere safe, like gold and a **paid-off house**.
Cut back, with no more holidays or new **car**.
feel: **Alarmed**, awake at night, feeling the ground has moved.
S2.quote: I did everything right, I worked hard and I saved, and the ground moves anyway. A family has to look after its own.
fieldNote: Pedro expects both his job and the family firm to be at risk within two years.
His response is **traditional**: close the circle, save, lean on the mosque and family.
His distress is about betrayal of the work-and-save deal, not money itself.

steps.text: Ask Mr. Hallam for a fair early retirement deal
Cut holidays and the new car and keep savings in safe assets
Lean on the mosque's family fund and the family if needed
Tell Omar and Samira to keep their jobs and savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a time to do right by people. I'd say Kestrel should promise its staff something, and the government should help family firms. At the mosque I'd say, let's make sure the young learn a trade as well as a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd manage to finish before it bites, at 63. I'd be fine. But Stuart would be running Kestrel and he'd be handing buying to the machine, and I'd hate to see the firm lose its name for service.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work to 62, then go. I'd use the time to teach the younger buyer, a girl called Rukhsana, the human parts of the trade, because that's what I can leave. I'd support an apprenticeship scheme through the mosque for the youngsters, and I'd put extra into the pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, a little, but I'd put it to one side. Five years feels like a stretch to prepare, and I'd say I'm better at preparing than at fretting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Stuart in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Stuart: if the machine buys the stock and you lose the shop owners' trust, you've lost the business. I'd say that politely, but I'd say it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the apprenticeship scheme involve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a machine buys your stock and the shop owners stop trusting Kestrel, you haven't saved money, you've lost your business. I'd say the same to anybody who'll listen.

say: I'd say five years is time to do **right** by people.
I'd say family firms need **government** help.
think: I'd finish at **63** before it bites, and I'd be fine.
I'd hate to see Kestrel lose its name for **service**.
do: Teach junior buyer **Rukhsana** the human parts of the trade.
Back an **apprenticeship** scheme through the mosque.
feel: **Anxious** a little, but better at preparing than fretting.
S3.quote: If a machine buys your stock and the shop owners stop trusting Kestrel, you haven't saved money, you've lost your business.
fieldNote: Pedro sees his own exit as safe but worries for the firm and for younger staff.
His **apprenticeship** plan matches his traditional outlook on work and community.
He tries to pass on trade knowledge to Rukhsana before he leaves.

steps.text: Work to 62 and teach Rukhsana the human side of buying
Back an apprenticeship scheme for local youngsters through the mosque

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a long time and it might never happen like they say. At the mosque I'd say, trust in God and build your children up. And at work I'd say that people in ten years will be glad we taught them to do things by hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it won't reach me. I'd be at home with a cup of tea. I'd worry for my grandchildren, who'll be adults then. I'd be calm for me and a bit uneasy about the world they'll inherit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work to 63, then retire. I'd put money into a fund for the grandchildren's education and training. I'd get involved with the mosque's youth work, teaching them to put things right with their hands, like fixing a bike.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. It's a long way off, like a storm cloud on the horizon, but it isn't over us yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children, Omar and Samira?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say to Omar and Samira, learn a trade that will always be needed: looking after people, repairing things, growing food. They know that, but I'd say it again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the youth work at the mosque involve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years from now my grandchildren will need to fix a bike and look after a neighbour, whatever the machines can do. I'd say that over a cup of tea and mean every word.

say: I'd say it's a long time and might never happen like they say.
I'd say people will be glad we taught them to work with their **hands**.
think: It won't reach me, as I'd be home with a cup of **tea**.
I worry about my **grandchildren** and the world they'll inherit.
do: Put money into a **fund** for the grandchildren's education and training.
Help with the mosque's **youth work** teaching practical skills.
feel: **Calm**, with a storm cloud on the horizon but not over us.
S4.quote: Ten years from now my grandchildren will need to fix a bike and look after a neighbour, whatever the machines can do.
fieldNote: Ten years puts his own career beyond reach, so he is mostly calm but uneasy about his **grandchildren**.
His faith and community guide his response.
He returns to practical skills as the safe side.

steps.text: Put money into a fund for the grandchildren's education
Help teach practical skills in the mosque's youth work

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. There's no time for the young to learn a trade or for the old to leave with dignity. What would help is a fair retirement deal, honest talk from the owners and support for family firms so they don't have to sell to the big ones.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not against progress. I'm not against progress, I'm against being told to throw away thirty years of knowing people as if it counted for nothing.

headlineQuote: I'm not against progress, I'm against being told to throw away thirty years of knowing people as if it counted for nothing.
portrait: Pedro is **58**, a hardware buyer at the family-owned Kestrel Hardware Wholesale, who refuses to use AI tools.
He's traditional, rooted in his **mosque** and family, and trusts voices and handshakes over screens.
With strong savings and a plan to retire at 62 or 63, he's calm when the change is slow.
He becomes anxious or **alarmed** when the change is fast, and leans on family, community and apprenticeships.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** world, with no time to leave with dignity or train the young.
whatWouldHelp: A fair **retirement** deal, honest owners and support for family firms.
